definitions.definition: For real s, H^s is the completion of trigonometric polynomials with norm squared sum_{k in Z} <k>^(2s)|fhat(k)|^2, <k>=(1+k^2)^(1/2). Negative spaces are distributions. L2=H^0 with normalized measure. On mean-zero distributions dot H^s has squared norm sum_{k!=0}|k|^(2s)|fhat(k)|^2. Smooth means spatially C-infinity. Real means fhat(-k)=conjugate(fhat(k)), and mean-zero means fhat(0)=0. Sequence ell2 uses counting measure. Time L-infinity norms are essential suprema, except time suprema of continuous representatives. Generic constants C may change; C_M depends only on gamma,T,M, never on a Fourier support bound or timestep.

inputs.statement: Babin–Ilyin–Titi primary results in their normalized mean-zero homogeneous spaces on R/(2 pi Z): write U_t=U U_x+U_xxx, Uhat(k)=exp(-it k^3) z_k(t), so z'_k=(ik/2) sum_{k1+k2=k}exp(3it k k1 k2)z_{k1}z_{k2}. A weak solution satisfies this integrated equation at every nonzero k. For every s>=0, B0>=0, horizon b>0 and initial z0 in dot H^s with ||z0||_2<=B0, the Galerkin equations z'_k=Pi_m[(ik/2) sum_{k1+k2=k} exp(3it k k1 k2)(Pi_m z)_{k1}(Pi_m z)_{k2}], z(0)=z0, have a bound sup_{[0,b]}||z^(m)||_{dot H^s}<=K_s(b,B0,||z0||_{dot H^s}), uniformly in m; the proof supplies a bound uniform when the indicated initial norm is bounded. For s>0 and 0<sigma<s, a subsequence converges strongly in L^p([0,b];dot H^sigma), 1<p<infinity, and weak-star in L-infinity dot H^s to a weak solution with the same bound and L2 conservation a.e.. This solution is unique and C([0,b];dot H^s), with Lipschitz continuous dependence in dot H^s, and conserves L2 at every time: for s>1/2 by the regular-solution uniqueness theorem, for 0<s<=1/2 by the positive rough-solution uniqueness theorem. For s=0 there is likewise a unique C([0,b];L2) weak solution with Lipschitz dependence. For any theta in (-1,0], and any two flows with ||z0||_2+||w0||_2<=B0, sup_{[0,b]}||z-w||_{dot H^theta}<=C' C_{B0}^b ||z0-w0||_{dot H^theta}, where C',C_{B0} depend only on B0,theta. The real, zero-mean class and normalized measure are standing conditions throughout.

output.statement: There is a finite A(T,gamma,R) uniform for every real mean-zero datum g with ||g||_{H^gamma}<=R. Its KdV equation u_t+u_xxx=(1/2)partial_x(u^2), u(0)=g, has a unique real mean-zero C([0,T];H^gamma) solution obtained by smooth approximation, solving the equation distributionally, with sup_t||u(t)||_{H^gamma}<=A. Smooth data give spatially smooth solutions. For v(t)=S_{-t}u(t), v'=B_t(v,v)/2 and all Sobolev norms of v and u agree. For two such exact flows with initial L2 norms summing to at most B0, sup_t||u-tilde u||_2<=C(T,B0)||g-tilde g||_2. In particular M=1+sup_t||v(t)||_{H^gamma}<=1+A uniformly.

argument.text: By H001, T>0 and 0<gamma<=1. For arbitrary real mean-zero g with ||g||_{H^gamma}<=R, reflection and sign give real mean-zero -g(-x) with the same Fourier norms. In particular its L2 and dot H^gamma norms are <=R. Instantiate E001 at s=gamma, b=T, B0=R and z0=-g(-x). Thus the equation U_t=U U_x+U_xxx admits a unique continuous dot H^gamma solution, and sup_{[0,T]}||U(t)||_{dot H^gamma}<=K_gamma(T,R,R), with K_gamma uniform over this ball. Smooth initial data belong to every positive integer Sobolev space; E001 at each such integer and uniqueness identify these regular solutions with the H^gamma solution, giving spatial smoothness. E001 at theta=0 and arbitrary two initial norms summing to at most B0 gives sup_{[0,T]}||U-Utilde||_2<=C(T,B0)||U(0)-Utilde(0)||_2.

produces.statement: For every real mean-zero g with ||g||_{H^gamma}<=R, there exists a unique C([0,T];dot H^gamma) solution of U_t=U U_x+U_xxx with U(0,x)=-g(-x), with a finite uniform homogeneous norm bound depending only on T,gamma,R. For smooth initial g this solution is spatially smooth. For any two real mean-zero initial data in this class whose initial L2 norms sum to at most B0, their corresponding source-sign flows satisfy sup_{[0,T]}||U-Utilde||_2<=C(T,B0)||U(0)-Utilde(0)||_2.

argument.text: Define \(u(t,x)=-U(t,-x)\). Then \(u_t=-U_t\), \(u_x=U_x\), \(u_{xxx}=U_{xxx}\) at \((t,-x)\), and consequently \(u_t+u_{xxx}=uu_x\). Fourier coefficients become \(\widehat u(k)=-\widehat U(-k)\), preserving every Sobolev norm, reality and zero mean. This transforms the source equation to u_t+u_xxx=(1/2)partial_x(u^2). The norm comparison above transfers all bounds to our \(H^\gamma\) norm. Hence there is \(A(T,\gamma,R)<\infty\) such that every smooth initial datum in the stated ball satisfies \(\sup_{[0,T]}\|u(t)\|_{H^\gamma}\le A\). The same bound holds for the limiting solution: for each finite set of frequencies pass to the limit in its finite norm sum, then take the supremum over finite sets. Thus \(M\le1+A(T,\gamma,R)\) uniformly. Continuous dependence in \(L^2\) is precisely the input used in the final density passage. No change of torus length or amplitude scaling is needed. More explicitly, the physical change u(t,x)=-U(t,-x) maps initial data g to source initial data -g(-x), so preserves the whole initial-data ball. The homogeneous-to-inhomogeneous inequalities follow coefficientwise from |k|<=<k><=sqrt(2)|k| for k!=0. For a continuous limiting flow the finite-frequency sums and then their supremum give the bound at each time, with the same constant. Apply the source pair bound after this isometry; it gives the stated C(T,B0) bound. Twisting by S_{-t} differentiates away -partial_x^3 and gives v'=B_t(v,v)/2. This proves all clauses of the output, for arbitrary data in the ball.

applications.bindings: Set source s=gamma, b=T, B0=R and source initial datum -g(-x). For continuity use 5.1 if gamma>1/2 and 6.3 otherwise; for smooth persistence use each positive integer s. For pairs set theta=0 and B0 to their initial norm sum bound.
hypothesis_checks: H001 gives T>0 and gamma>0; real mean-zero data g in the ball remain real mean-zero with the same norms after sign/reflection. Their L2 and dot H^gamma norms are <=R by coefficientwise norm comparison. For smooth data every integer Sobolev norm is finite, so uniqueness identifies those regular flows.
theta=0 belongs to (-1,0]. The two initial L2 norms are, by the universally stated pair condition, bounded in sum by B0. Reflection preserves this sum.
